                    ### Question
                    A 16-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a follow-up of a wound on his ankle. He had a pedestrian accident 3 days ago which caused a skin defect on the dorsal side of his left ankle. The lesion was cleaned, debrided, and observed over the past 3 days. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no signs of local infection. A photograph of the lesion is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical management?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Free tissue transfer flap
opb. Full-thickness skin graft
opc. Musculocutaneous flap
opd. Primary closure
ope. Split-thickness skin graft

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
In the management of a wound on the ankle with no signs of infection, the choice of surgical intervention depends on the size and complexity of the skin defect. For small defects, primary closure is often appropriate, as it allows for direct approximation of wound edges. For moderate defects where primary closure is not feasible, a split-thickness skin graft is typically used due to its ability to cover larger areas and promote healing. Full-thickness skin grafts are reserved for larger defects requiring more durable coverage. Complex defects, especially those involving exposed bone or tendon, may necessitate more advanced techniques such as a free tissue transfer flap or a musculocutaneous flap, which provide robust coverage and vascular supply. The retrieved evidence path mentioning 'myocutaneous flap' aligns with the consensus that such flaps are used for complex defects involving deeper structures. Given the absence of infection and the typical nature of ankle wounds, a split-thickness skin graft is likely the most appropriate choice for a moderate defect, balancing coverage needs and surgical complexity.
